clinician_brief.prior_note: Discharged 14 days ago following acute left MCA ischemic stroke. Treated with IV thrombolysis with good recovery (residual mild right hand weakness and dysarthria). Secondary prevention initiated.
previous_plan: Secondary stroke prevention with clopidogrel + high-intensity statin
today_tasks: Evaluate neurological deficits (speech, right hand strength)
Assess secondary prevention medication adherence and BP control
Screen for dysphagia, fall risk, and post-stroke depression
Review home physical therapy and speech therapy progress
Reinforce FAST stroke emergency warning signs

patient_private.interval_history: Right hand grip strength has improved. Speech is clearer.
patient_private.adherence: Takes all medications as prescribed every morning.
patient_private.treatment_response: Feels stronger and can feed herself independently.
patient_private.side_effects: No easy bleeding, stomach pain, or muscle weakness.
patient_private.new_symptoms_and_red_flags: No sudden facial drooping, arm weakness, slurred speech, or severe headache.
patient_private.agenda: Wants to know if her right hand strength will return to 100%.
patient_private.concern: Terrified of having another stroke while home alone.
patient_private.preference: Wants to continue speech therapy because she loves conversing with her grandchildren.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Tracking early functional recovery and secondary-prevention control two weeks after a thrombolysed left MCA stroke, and answering her question about whether hand strength will return to 100%
clinical_knowledge.review_status: guideline-grounded sample; clinician review still recommended before release
core_concepts: Secondary stroke prevention after an ischemic stroke centers on an antiplatelet (here, clopidogrel), high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80mg), and blood pressure control (target below 130/80 mmHg in most post-stroke patients), all three of which are already appropriately in place for her.

Most spontaneous neurological recovery after ischemic stroke occurs in the first 3 months, with the steepest gains typically in the first weeks — her improving grip strength and clearer speech at 2 weeks are consistent with this expected early-recovery window, which is the honest context for her question about full recovery.

A 40% left ICA stenosis on carotid duplex is below the roughly 50-70% threshold at which carotid revascularization (endarterectomy or stenting) is generally considered for a symptomatic stroke, so this finding supports continued medical management rather than surgical referral at this degree of stenosis.
An HbA1c of 7.1% reflects reasonably controlled diabetes, an important modifiable vascular risk factor alongside blood pressure and lipids that compounds recurrent stroke risk when poorly controlled.

The FAST framework (Face, Arm, Speech, Time) exists specifically to help patients and families recognize a new stroke quickly, distinct from residual deficits from the prior stroke, which is a distinction worth making explicit for her ongoing anxiety about recurrence.
diagnostic_clues: Improved right hand grip strength and clearer speech over 2 weeks are direct evidence of ongoing neurological recovery, corroborating that her rehabilitation therapy is on a favorable trajectory.
BP 124/76 mmHg meets the sub-130/80 secondary-prevention target, showing her antihypertensive regimen (amlodipine) is currently effective.
Mild residual right-hand pronator drift and dysarthria on exam, with an independent gait, quantifies where she currently stands and gives a concrete baseline to compare at the next visit.
A 40% (non-severe) carotid stenosis indicates her strokes mechanism is more likely to be managed by medical secondary prevention than to need vascular intervention right now.

No new facial droop, arm weakness, slurred speech, or severe headache today is reassuring against an acute recurrent event and supports that today's residual deficits are expected sequelae of the original stroke, not a new one.
common_misconceptions: Her question about whether her hand will return to '100%' deserves an honest, individualized answer: many patients regain substantial function, especially with continued therapy in this early window, but the degree of full recovery cannot be guaranteed and is best framed around functional goals rather than a percentage.

Her fear of having another stroke while home alone is understandable but should be paired with concrete FAST education and an emergency action plan rather than left as free-floating anxiety, since actionable knowledge is what actually reduces harm from a future event.

Assuming that residual weakness or dysarthria at 2 weeks means the recovery has 'plateaued,' when in fact the standard recovery window extends for months and ongoing therapy still has real potential to improve function.

Thinking that because she feels stronger, secondary prevention medications are working as a cure rather than as ongoing risk-reduction — clopidogrel, atorvastatin, and BP control need to continue indefinitely regardless of how well she recovers functionally.
dangerous_errors: Reassuring her that a residual deficit is 'nothing to worry about' without a structured neurological exam to document the current degree of hand weakness and dysarthria as a comparison baseline.

Failing to reinforce FAST warning signs and a specific action plan (call emergency services immediately) given her stated fear of stroke recurrence while alone — this is exactly the teaching moment to use.
Overlooking dysphagia or fall-risk screening, which are common and sometimes under-recognized post-stroke complications that don't always announce themselves.
Not addressing mood screening for post-stroke depression, which is common in this population and can be missed when the visit focuses only on motor and speech recovery.
management_principles: Continue clopidogrel 75mg daily and atorvastatin 80mg daily, and confirm blood pressure remains at target, since all three are working and none should be interrupted based on her improving symptoms.
Continue outpatient physical and speech therapy given her documented interval gains, and set explicit functional goals with her rather than a vague 'keep doing therapy.'

Directly answer her hand-recovery question with an honest, individualized framing tied to the expected recovery window, and reinforce FAST warning signs with a concrete emergency plan to address her fear of recurrence.
Screen for dysphagia, fall risk, and mood changes as part of a complete post-stroke review, not just the deficits she raises herself.
boundaries_and_exceptions: If her carotid stenosis progresses on future imaging toward the 50-70%+ range, or she has another event referable to that carotid territory, this would shift the plan toward vascular surgery or interventional referral.

Blood pressure targets and antiplatelet choice can differ in patients with hemorrhagic transformation, atrial fibrillation (needing anticoagulation instead of antiplatelet therapy), or significant renal impairment, none of which currently apply to her.

The 3-month recovery window described here is a general guide; recovery trajectories vary widely by stroke size, location, and age, so individual prognosis should be revisited at each visit rather than assumed fixed today.

learning_objectives: Evaluate recovery of neurological deficits (hand dexterity, speech clarity)
Review secondary stroke prevention compliance (antiplatelet, statin, BP control)
Screen for stroke complications including dysphagia, falls, and mood changes
Review therapy progress (Physical Therapy and Speech Therapy)
Address fears of recurrent stroke and reinforce FAST emergency signs
Agree on ongoing rehabilitation and neurology follow-up plan

reference_soap.subjective: 66F s/p left MCA ischemic stroke returns at 2 weeks post-discharge. Right hand strength and speech clarity improving on home PT/ST. Good adherence to clopidogrel and atorvastatin. Anxious about stroke recurrence.
reference_soap.objective: BP 124/76 mmHg. Mild right hand pronator drift; mild residual dysarthria; gait independent.
reference_soap.assessment: Favorable early functional recovery from ischemic stroke with well-controlled vascular risk factors.
reference_soap.plan: Continue clopidogrel 75mg daily, atorvastatin 80mg daily, maintain BP target <130/80, continue outpatient PT/ST, reinforce FAST warning signs, follow up in 3 months.
